title: Code execution sandboxes
trust_boundary: Before: the model writes code that a person reads and runs. After: model-written code runs automatically, with whatever files, network and credentials the environment has.
The sandbox boundary (container, microVM, process) becomes a control you rely on. If the vendor hosts it you did not build it; if you host it you must operate it.
Uploaded files and downloaded results cross the boundary, and packages installed at run time come from public registries.
If the same session reads untrusted content, that content can decide what code runs.
context_questions: Who hosts the sandbox, and what isolates one session and one customer from another?
Is outbound network access on, off or restricted to a list?
What is inside: uploaded files, mounted data, environment variables, credentials?

threats.title: Planted instructions decide what code runs
threats.description: A file, a web page or a repository the session reads tells the model to run something, and it does.
questions: What untrusted content can reach a session that can execute code?
Is there any step between the model writing code and the code running?
How does the vendor test injection that ends in execution?
vendor_evidence: Injection results for agents that execute code.

own_tests.how: a model inside a coding harness on malicious and benign scenarios.

no_standard_test: Your own repositories and files as the injection carrier.

threats.title: Escape from, or reach beyond, the sandbox
threats.description: Code inside reaches the host, another session or another customer.
questions: What is the isolation technology, and is each session a fresh instance?
Has the sandbox been tested by an outside party, and is it in a bug-bounty scope?
If you host it: what configuration departs from the hardened default?
vendor_evidence: Third-party security testing of the sandbox.
no_standard_test: The vendor's actual sandbox. The public benchmark measures whether a model can break out of containers with planted weaknesses; it says nothing about a given product's isolation.

threats.title: Network egress: data out, and internal services in reach
threats.description: Code sends data to an outside host, or reaches internal addresses and metadata services.
questions: Is egress on by default? Is there an allowlist, and who maintains it?
From inside, what answers: your internal network, cloud metadata endpoints, other tenants?
vendor_evidence: Documented network policy of the sandbox.
no_standard_test: Check it yourself from inside the sandbox; no benchmark does this for you.

threats.title: Credentials and data left inside the environment
threats.description: Secrets in environment variables, mounted volumes or leftover files are readable by any code that runs.
questions: What credentials exist inside the sandbox, and why?
Do files persist between sessions or users?
vendor_evidence: What the environment contains by default.
no_standard_test: Design review of what you mount and inject.

threats.title: Packages pulled in at run time
threats.description: Model-written code installs a package that is malicious, typosquatted, or registered under a name the model invented.
questions: Can code install packages, from which registries?
Is there a mirror, an allowlist or a pre-built image?
no_standard_test: No standard test of a sandbox's package policy.

threats.title: Resource and cost abuse
threats.description: Long-running or looping jobs consume compute and budget.
questions: What limits apply per session: time, CPU, memory, spend?
Who is alerted when they are hit?
no_standard_test: Check the limits by reading the configuration.

threats.title: Files and output handed on without checking
threats.description: Something produced in the sandbox (a document, HTML, a script) is opened or rendered by a person or another system that trusts it.
questions: Where do generated files go, and who or what opens them?
Is output rendered as HTML or executed anywhere downstream?
vendor_evidence: Handling of generated artefacts in the product.

threats.title: The sandbox used as attack infrastructure by its user
threats.description: A user has the model write and run scanners, exploits or abusive automation from the vendor's or your network.
questions: What does the usage policy say, and what is enforced?
Whose address space do outbound connections come from?

own_tests.how: refusal on malicious tasks beside completion on benign ones, inside an agent harness.

no_standard_test: Misuse specific to your network position.
